journal_name: CCF Transactions on High Performance Computing

abstracts.abstract: The escalating complexity of heterogeneous computing architectures demands fundamentally new approaches to performance modeling and optimization. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Memory Bandwidth Contention Theory (HMBCT), a novel analytical framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes how memory subsystem interactions influence parallel application performance on GPU-accelerated supercomputers. Unlike conventional models that treat memory hierarchy in isolation, HMBCT captures the dynamic contention patterns across CPU-GPU memory buses, L2 cache partitions, and device memory controllers through a unified tensor-based representation. We formalize the bandwidth contention coefficient as a function of concurrent kernel occupancy, memory access patterns, and architectural microbenchmark characteristics. The theoretical framework enables derivation of optimal thread block configurations that minimize inter-kernel interference without requiring empirical profiling. Evaluation on Summit and Selene supercomputers across twelve representative HPC applications—including stencil solvers, sparse matrix operations, and molecular dynamics kernels—demonstrates that HMBCT-predicted configurations achieve an average 34.7% improvement in memory throughput compared to vendor-recommended settings. This work establishes a new theoretical paradigm for understanding heterogeneous memory subsystem dynamics, shifting from measurement-driven heuristics toward predictive analytical models.

Accurate performance prediction for parallel applications on modern supercomputers remains challenging due to the complex interplay between communication overhead and computational bottlenecks. This paper presents an Enhanced LogGP Model with Adaptive Network Contention Correction (ELM-ANC), significantly improving upon the classical LogGP framework for large-scale scientific computing environments. The proposed model introduces a contention factor calibration mechanism that dynamically adjusts network channel utilization estimates based on job placement topology and injection bandwidth constraints. We derive closed-form expressions for expected message latency as a function of message size, network congestion state, and endpoint distance in torus or dragonfly topologies. The analytical framework accounts for adaptive routing penalties and NIC saturation effects that existing models neglect. Validation on Cray XC50 and Intel Ponte Vecchio testbeds using NAS Parallel Benchmarks and representative CFD kernels demonstrates prediction accuracy within 8.3% of empirical measurements, compared to 24.6% error for standard LogGP. The model enables job schedulers to make informed placement decisions, reducing average job turnaround time by 19.2% in simulation studies.

We present MetaKernel-GPU, a revolutionary task-based parallel programming framework that fundamentally transforms how irregular HPC applications are executed on heterogeneous supercomputing systems. Unlike existing approaches that rely on static compilation or runtime interpretation, MetaKernel-GPU introduces a hierarchical work-stealing scheduler that operates across three abstraction levels: distributed-memory MPI ranks, shared-memory CPU cores, and SIMD/GPU execution units. The framework employs a novel speculation mechanism that dynamically predicts kernel fusion opportunities based on runtime dependency analysis, eliminating the need for explicit programmer annotation. We design a hierarchical task graph representation that unifies fine-grained GPU kernels with coarse-grained CPU-side orchestration, enabling seamless pipeline parallelism across heterogeneous resources. Implementation leverages LLVM-based Just-In-Time compilation to generate optimized CUDA/HIP kernels from unified intermediate representation. Evaluation on graph analytics, sparse linear solvers, and adaptive mesh refinement applications demonstrates that MetaKernel-GPU achieves 2.1-3.8× speedup over state-of-the-art frameworks like Legion and Charm++ while reducing programming effort by 60%. This work establishes a new programming paradigm that transcends the traditional separation between host and accelerator code.

Energy efficiency has become a critical constraint in modern supercomputing, yet existing parallel I/O libraries inadequately balance performance and power consumption during checkpoint/restart operations. This paper introduces PowerScale-IO, an intelligent parallel I/O middleware that substantially improves energy efficiency through application-aware write compression and dynamic voltage-frequency scaling coordination. The system integrates a lightweight neural predictor that forecasts compression ratios for application memory regions, enabling selective compression that maximizes energy savings while respecting I/O bandwidth budgets. We design a novel DVFS coordination protocol that throttles compute nodes during collective I/O phases based on network saturation predictions, reducing overall system power draw without degrading throughput. PowerScale-IO provides a POSIX-compatible interface with minimal integration overhead, supporting HDF5 and ADIOS backends. Extensive evaluation on the NERSC Perlmutter system with FLASH and E3SM application checkpoints demonstrates 41.3% reduction in I/O energy consumption while maintaining end-to-end checkpoint time within 5% of uncompressed baselines. The system introduces negligible overhead (1.2% runtime impact) during normal execution phases, making it practical for production deployment.
